title: Darkness That Can Be Felt
theme: Locusts devour what the hail left, and then a thick darkness covers Egypt for three days while Israel has light. Pharaoh tries to limit Israel's departure, first leaving the children and then the flocks, but Moses insists that all must go to serve the LORD. God does all this so that Israel will tell their children that he is the LORD.

language.note: 'That you may tell in the hearing of your son and your grandson.' The plagues are not only judgment on Egypt but a story for Israel's children. Retelling God's acts to the next generation becomes a command at Passover (12:26-27; 13:8, 14).
The swarming desert locust, from a root meaning 'to multiply.' A swarm can strip a land bare in hours. Joel later uses a locust plague as a picture of the day of the LORD.

The darkness of Genesis 1:2 before God said 'Let there be light.' Egypt is plunged back into pre-creation darkness while Israel has light, as if creation itself is being reversed for Egypt and preserved for Israel.

language.gloss: to deal harshly, make a fool of
language.note: 'How I have dealt harshly with the Egyptians' can also mean 'how I made a fool of Egypt.' God has exposed the pretensions of Egypt's king and gods.

usage.note: God's saving acts are to be passed down from parent to child so that each generation will set its hope in God.
Joel's locusts are an army of the day of the LORD, and Revelation's fifth trumpet releases demonic locusts from the abyss.
Darkness covers the earth, but the LORD rises on his people. Jesus is the light of the world, and God has delivered believers from the domain of darkness.

context.setting: The eighth and ninth plagues complete the third round. Pharaoh's officials, worn down by ruin, urge him to let Israel go. The darkness strikes at the sun god Ra (Re), the chief god of Egypt, of whom Pharaoh was considered the son.

flow.label: Why God does this
flow.note: God has hardened Pharaoh's heart so that he can show his signs and so that Israel will tell their children and grandchildren and know that he is the LORD.

flow.label: Who will go?
flow.note: Moses warns of locusts. Pharaoh's servants beg him to relent. Pharaoh offers to let only the men go; Moses insists on young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds. Moses and Aaron are driven out.

flow.label: Locusts
flow.note: An east wind brings locusts that cover the land and eat every plant left by the hail. Pharaoh confesses and asks for prayer; a west wind drives the locusts into the Red Sea. The LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart.

flow.label: Darkness
flow.note: Unannounced, thick darkness covers Egypt for three days, but Israel has light. Pharaoh offers to let all the people go if they leave their flocks. Moses refuses; Pharaoh threatens Moses with death if he sees his face again.

tier1.note: He sent darkness and made the land dark; he spoke, and the locusts came without number and devoured every plant.
He gave their crops to the caterpillar and their produce to the locust.

tier2.note: The fifth bowl plunges the beast's kingdom into darkness, and people gnaw their tongues in anguish yet do not repent.
Joel describes a locust army darkening the land as a picture of the coming day of the LORD.
Darkness covered the land for three hours while Jesus hung on the cross, bearing God's judgment.

tier3.note: God called his people out of darkness into his marvelous light.
Teach God's words diligently to your children as you sit, walk, lie down and rise.
Jesus refuses partial discipleship, just as Moses refused partial obedience.

voices.name: Philip Graham Ryken
voices.view: Ryken applies Moses' insistence that the children go too (v9) to Christian families. God's people are not to leave their children behind in Egypt; worship is a family calling, and the story of salvation is meant to be told to sons and grandsons.

voices.name: Matthew Henry
voices.view: Henry sees in the darkness that could be felt a picture of the spiritual darkness of sin, and in the light in Israel's dwellings a picture of the light God gives his people even when the world around them is dark.

translations.kjv: And the LORD said unto Moses, Stretch out thine hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt.
translations.note: The Hebrew uses the verb for groping in the dark (as in Deuteronomy 28:29). The darkness was so thick it seemed physical. Some suggest a severe sandstorm was involved; the text stresses that it covered Egypt but not Israel's homes.

translations.kjv: And he said unto them, Let the LORD be so with you, as I will let you go, and your little ones: look to it; for evil is before you.

renderings.text: you have some evil purpose in mind
Clearly you are bent on evil

translations.note: Pharaoh's sarcastic 'May the LORD be with you' is followed by an accusation. Some see a pun on Ra, the sun god, since the Hebrew word for evil (ra) sounds like it: 'Ra is against you.' The darkness plague soon answers him.

steps.gospel: Egypt sits in darkness that can be felt while Israel has light in their dwellings. When Jesus hung on the cross, darkness covered the land, because the light of the world was bearing the judgment of darkness for his people. Now God has 'delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son.' Moses refused to leave anyone or anything behind, and Christ likewise came to redeem his whole people, young and old, and to claim all of life for God.
application: Tell your children and grandchildren what God has done. The plagues were meant to be retold at the table.
Refuse to leave any part of your life in Egypt: children, possessions, time or plans. God claims it all.
Do not be fooled by Pharaoh's bargains: worship with conditions he sets is not freedom.
Take courage that God's people can have light even when darkness covers the world around them.

misapplications.claim: It is enough for the adults of a family to follow God; children can decide later.
misapplications.correction: Moses insisted 'We will go with our young and our old, with our sons and daughters' (v9). The children belonged to the covenant community and joined the worship.

misapplications.claim: Pharaoh's offers show he was gradually becoming reasonable.
misapplications.correction: Each offer was meant to keep a hold on Israel: hostages in the children, then property in the flocks. Partial release kept Israel bound to Egypt.

contrasts.note: The clearest separation yet; one land, two experiences.
Pharaoh's partial freedom against God's full deliverance.
Even his officials see Egypt is ruined, but Pharaoh cannot bend.

features.label: The east and west winds
features.note: An east wind brings the locusts and a west wind removes them into the Red Sea (Yam Suph). The next time a wind blows over that sea, Israel will walk through it.

features.label: Unannounced darkness
features.note: As the third plague of the third round, darkness comes without warning, like the gnats (8:16) and the boils (9:8).

features.label: Three days
features.note: Pharaoh would not let Israel go three days into the wilderness to worship, so Egypt sits three days in darkness.

features.label: Last face-to-face
features.note: Pharaoh says Moses will die if he sees his face again; Moses replies 'I will not see your face again' (v29). The negotiations are over.

steps.summary: Exodus 10 brings the plagues to the edge of the climax. Locusts destroy Egypt's food and darkness covers its land, while Israel has light. Pharaoh's attempts at partial release fail, because God claims all of his people and their possessions for worship. Behind it all stands God's purpose: that Israel will tell their children that he is the LORD.

metaArc.book: Chapter 10 completes the nine plagues and ends all negotiation with Pharaoh, leaving only the final blow in chapters 11-12. Its call to tell the next generation shapes the Passover instructions.
metaArc.redemptive: The plunge of Egypt into darkness and the light of Israel point to the separation of light and darkness in Christ's redemption, and to the final day when God's people walk in his light.
